About: Exploring the Standard Model

What this is
This simulation lays out the particle content of the Standard Model of particle physics — every quark, lepton, gauge boson and the Higgs, on one table. Recolour the tiles by Family, Charge or Mass to bring out a different pattern each time, and read the log-scale mass ladder beneath to get a feel for how enormously the masses differ. Click any tile for its mass, charge, spin and year of discovery, or switch the view to Lagrangian to see the single equation that encodes all their interactions.
Concept
The Standard Model: 17 fundamental particles — 6 quarks, 6 leptons, 4 gauge bosons and 1 Higgs — plus one compact Lagrangian encoding all their interactions. Every number shown (mass, charge, spin, discovery year) is a measured, experimentally verified value.
Units
Masses are quoted as energies through E = mc², so “0.511 MeV” is shorthand for 0.511 MeV/c². One electronvolt (eV) is the energy an electron picks up crossing a 1-volt drop, and the prefixes are just powers of ten: 1 MeV = 10⁶ eV, 1 GeV = 10⁹ eV, 1 TeV = 10¹² eV. The ladder therefore spans more than eleven decades, from neutrinos below 1 eV to the top quark at 172.6 GeV.
Serves
Summarize the Standard Model theory and explain what it means for a theory to be "experimentally well-tested": each tile carries a discovery year and precision-measured properties spanning 1897–2012, from cathode-ray tubes to the LHC.
Inquiry
Which particles are familiar and which are new? Recolor the same tiles by charge or by mass: electric charges repeat identically across the three generations, while masses grow enormously — and the log-scale mass ladder makes that pattern quantitative.
Misconception
"The Higgs, being the newest and most famous discovery, must be the heaviest particle." In fact the top quark (172.6 GeV) outweighs the Higgs (125.2 GeV); the predict question confronts this directly on the mass ladder.
PrincipleWhere it appears
Prediction before revelationThe sidebar asks for the heaviest particle before the mass ladder settles the question; feedback names the gap between guess and measurement.
Misconception as a choice"The famous Higgs must be heaviest" is one of the answer chips; choosing it triggers the rebuttal — the top quark outweighs it by roughly 47 GeV.
Invariant vs. varyingRecoloring the same tiles by charge reveals a pattern that never changes across generations; recoloring by mass shows the quantity that varies by many orders of magnitude.
Operational anchorsEvery claim is a labelled measured number on screen: masses, charges, spins and discovery years from 1897 to 2012.
Formal layer on demandThe condensed Lagrangian expands term-by-term on hover/click; the full revision sheet — chapters, typeset equations, computed diagrams and a live worked example — opens from the ⚛︎ The Physics button.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Seventeen particles

Let’s get our bearings. Columns I–III are the matter particles, and the gauge column holds the force carriers. You’ll find the masses of all these particles marked on a logarithmic scale at the bottom of the screen.

2 · Three generations

Each column of matter particles is called a generation. Have a look along the rows — when you go from one generation to the next, what do you think changes?

3 · Newest, so heaviest?

Now for a tempting shortcut. Heavier particles are harder to produce, and the last particle we found was the Higgs boson. So is it the heaviest? What do you think?

The Physics

The Standard Model · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim lays out the 17 particles of the Standard Model as one table and ties them to the Lagrangian, the equation that governs them. You can recolour the table, switch matter to antimatter, open a mass scale and read each particle's card.

What you'll learn

  • How the 17 particles group into matter, force carriers and the Higgs.
  • How charge and mass vary along the rows and columns of the table.
  • What each term of the Lagrangian does.
  • How the Higgs field enters the masses of the fermions, the W and the Z.
The table's layout: matter in columns I–III, then the force carriers, then the Higgs. Colours are the sim's Family colours.

What's on screen

  • Quarks (purple): the top two rows of columns I–III.
  • Leptons (green): the bottom two rows, the charged leptons e, μ, τ and the three neutrinos.
  • Gauge bosons (red): the force carriers g, γ, Z and W.
  • The Higgs (gold), alone in the last column. It is selected when the sim opens.
  • Card (right): the selected tile's mass, charge, spin, colour, weak isospin, hypercharge and year found.
  • Mass ladder (bottom, when Mass log scale is on): masses on a log axis from 0.1 MeV to 1 TeV, with a separate box for the massless particles and the neutrinos (< 1 eV).
See itShow the table in Family colours with the Higgs selected. Watch for: tiles in four colours, the Higgs tile ringed, and its card on the right.

03

Fields in the table, terms in the Lagrangian

Each tile is a field, and the table groups them by role. Twelve are matter: six quarks and six leptons. Four carry forces: the gluon (strong), the photon (electromagnetic) and the W and Z (weak). The last is the Higgs. The g tile stands for eight gluons and the W tile for W⁺ and W⁻.

  • Quarks feel the strong, electromagnetic and weak forces.
  • The charged leptons e, μ and τ feel the electromagnetic and weak forces.
  • Neutrinos feel only the weak force.

The Lagrangian ℒ writes all of this as one equation. Its five terms are the five chips of the sim's Lagrangian view; click a chip and the panel names the term and says what it does.

Indices and gauge fixing are suppressed. h.c. is the hermitian conjugate of the Yukawa term.
See itOpen the Lagrangian view with the matter term selected. Watch for: five chips across the top, the one labelled "matter & forces" lit, and its panel titled "Matter in motion" below.
04

Generations are heavier copies

Columns I, II and III are the three generations. Along each row of matter tiles the charge is the same: u, c, t carry +⅔; d, s, b carry −⅓; e, μ, τ carry −1; the neutrinos carry 0. Spin is ½ ħ in every matter tile. What changes from column to column is the mass.

The sim's Charge colours, with the catalogue masses.
  • From the electron (0.511 MeV) to the top (172.6 GeV) is about five and a half decades of mass.
  • The top is the heaviest particle in the table. It outweighs the Higgs (125.2 GeV), the Z (91.19 GeV) and the W (80.37 GeV).
  • The Standard Model contains the three copies but does not explain why there are three, or why their masses differ so much.
See itRecolour the table by charge. Watch for: one colour along each row, the same in all three columns: orange +⅔, teal −⅓, blue −1, grey 0.
See itColour by mass and open the log ladder with the top quark selected. Watch for: the top, at 172.6 GeV, furthest right on the ladder, past the W, the Higgs and the Z.
05

Each force reads its own charge

In the Lagrangian, the derivative Dμ is where matter meets the forces. Each force field multiplies one kind of charge: G reads colour (strength gs), W reads weak isospin (g) and B reads hypercharge (g′).

Quarks feel all three couplings; neutrinos, with no colour and no electric charge, feel only g and g′.

Electric charge is a mix of two of them, and it is what the card's rows add up to:

The identity under every fermion's card: Q = T₃ + ½Y.
  • Each quark and charged lepton has a left-chiral (L) and a right-chiral (R) part. The weak force acts only on the L part, which has T = ½. The R part has T = 0.
  • The L | R chip shows both. The electron has T₃ = −½, Y = −1 (L) and T₃ = 0, Y = −2 (R). Q = −1 either way.
  • Antimatter flips the signs of Q, T₃ and Y. The mass does not change.
See itSelect the electron and flip its chirality from L to R. Watch for: T₃ and Y changing on the card while Q stays −1.
06

Fermion masses come from the Higgs field

A fermion gets its mass from a Yukawa term, a coupling y between the fermion (L̄ and fR) and the Higgs field φ. Once φ takes its value v = 246 GeV, the coupling is the mass:

The sim uses v = 246 GeV.
Particle Chirality Fermions Ladder

Pick a fermion to see its y. These controls move the sim too.

  • y is proportional to the mass. The top has y = 0.99 and the electron y = 2.9 × 10⁻⁶, so the spread of masses is a spread of couplings.
  • The Standard Model predicts none of the y values. Each is measured and put into the equation.
  • The neutrinos have no Yukawa term here, because the model has no right-chiral neutrino. Their masses are tiny but not zero, and need an extension.
See itOpen the Yukawa term with the top quark selected. Watch for: a panel titled "Yukawa couplings" under the chips, and y = 0.99 for the top in the card.
07

The Higgs field's value gives the W and Z their mass

The potential has a negative μ² term, so φ = 0 is a hilltop. The field settles on the brim of the hat, at v = 246 GeV.

The Higgs mass fixes λ and μ: for mH = 125.2 GeV, λ = 0.13 and μ = 88.5 GeV.

With φ nonzero, the term |Dμφ|² gives the W and Z their masses:

cos θW is the weak mixing angle.
  • mW = 80.37 GeV gives g = 0.653. mZ = 91.19 GeV gives √(g² + g′²) = 0.741, so cos θW = mW/mZ = 0.881.
  • The photon is the mix of W³ and B that the field's value leaves alone, so it stays massless. The gluon stays massless because colour is never broken.
See itOpen the Higgs potential term. Watch for: a panel titled "Higgs potential" saying the field settles at 246 GeV. In a wide window it also draws the hat.
See itOpen the W, Z masses term. Watch for: the "W, Z masses" chip lit, and a panel saying the photon stays massless.
08

Where it matters

  • The Higgs discovery. In 2012 ATLAS and CMS at the LHC found the Higgs boson, at 125.2 GeV. Measuring how strongly it couples to each particle tests the Yukawa picture of section 06.
  • A short-range weak force. The W and Z masses limit the weak force's range to about ħ/(mWc) ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁸ m, far smaller than a proton.
  • The Sun. Its first fusion step, p + p → d + e⁺ + ν, is a weak process, so it runs slowly and the Sun burns for billions of years.
Go deeper: what this table leaves out
  • As drawn here the neutrinos are massless. Oscillation experiments show they are not, so the model needs an extension.
  • Gravity is not in the Standard Model, and neither is a particle for dark matter.
  • The masses, the three gauge couplings and the mixing between generations are all inputs, measured and not predicted.
09

Summary

In one line. Matter comes in three heavier-and-heavier copies that feel the same forces, and the Higgs field's value of 246 GeV turns couplings into masses.

Key points

  • The 17 tiles are 12 matter fields, 4 force carriers and the Higgs.
  • Along a row, charge and spin repeat and mass grows. The top (172.6 GeV) is the heaviest tile.
  • Q = T₃ + ½Y. The L and R parts of a fermion have different T₃ and Y.
  • With v = 246 GeV, m = y v/√2 for fermions, mW = ½ g v and mZ = ½ √(g² + g′²) v. The photon and gluon stay massless.

Common mix-ups

  • "The last particle found is the heaviest." The Higgs, found in 2012, is 125.2 GeV. The top, found in 1995, is 172.6 GeV.
  • "The Higgs field gives matter all its mass." It gives the fermions, W and Z their masses. Most of a proton's mass is strong-force energy: its quark masses add up to about 1 %.
  • "An antiparticle has the opposite mass." The mass is the same. Q, T₃ and Y flip.

Things to try on your own

  • Colour by Charge, then switch Fermions to Antimatter. List which tiles change colour and which do not.
  • Select the electron, then the top, and compare their y values in section 06 with their masses.
  • Select the up quark and flip L to R. Check Q = T₃ + ½Y for both.
